Number Systems

Hexadecimal

Year 10, 1.1 L3

steps.label: Hex to Denary
steps.content:
Hex to Denary

  • Hexadecimal is base 16. It uses the digits 0 to 9, then the letters A to F for the values 10 to 15.
  • One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, so two hex digits fit in one byte.
  • The left digit is worth ×16. The right digit is worth ×1.
  • Add the two column values together to get the denary total.

steps.label: Denary to Hex
steps.content:
Denary to Hex

  • Divide the denary number by 16 and keep only the whole number part. That is the left digit.
  • Multiply that digit by 16 and subtract it from the original number. What is left is the right digit.
  • Any digit above 9 is written as a letter, A for 10 up to F for 15.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What denary value does the hex digit F represent?
  • Why is hexadecimal described as base 16?
  • What column value is the left digit of a 2-digit hex number worth?
  • How many bits fit into one hex digit?
  • Why might a programmer prefer writing FF over 11111111?

steps.label: Hex to Binary
steps.content:
Hex to Binary

  • Each hex digit converts to its own group of 4 bits.
  • Convert every digit separately, then join the groups in the same order as the original hex number.
  • Each group is always written as 4 digits, padding with 0s on the left if needed.
  • A register with more hex digits just needs more 4-bit groups. The method does not change.

steps.label: Binary to Hex
steps.content:
Binary to Hex

  • Split the binary number into groups of 4 bits, starting from the right.
  • If the leftmost group has fewer than 4 bits, pad it with 0s on the left first.
  • Convert each group to its hex digit separately.
  • Join the converted digits in the same order as the groups.

  • Which direction do you split a binary number into groups of 4?
  • What do you do with a group that has fewer than 4 bits?
  • How many bits does a 3-digit hex number represent?
  • Why is hex a more compact way to write a binary value than binary itself?
